questions.question: What is an Amazon Machine Image (AMI)?
questions.answer: An AMI is a template that contains everything needed to launch an EC2 instance — the operating system, application software, configuration settings, and EBS snapshot references. It acts as the blueprint for servers, allowing you to launch identical instances repeatedly.

questions.question: What are the three main sources of AMIs in the EC2 launch wizard?
questions.answer: The three sources are: (1) Quick Start AMIs — clean OS images maintained by AWS with the latest security patches; (2) My AMIs — custom AMIs you created from your own EC2 instances; (3) AWS Marketplace AMIs — third-party vendor images, often with commercial software pre-installed, some with additional licensing fees.

questions.question: What is the relationship between an EBS Volume, an EBS Snapshot, and an AMI?
questions.answer: An EBS Volume is the live virtual hard disk attached to a running EC2 instance. An EBS Snapshot is a point-in-time backup of that volume — it captures only the used data. An AMI is a higher-level template that references EBS snapshots and adds launch configuration metadata. When you create a custom AMI, AWS automatically creates an EBS snapshot of the root volume in the background.

questions.question: Are AMIs global resources in AWS?
questions.answer: No. AMIs are region-specific resources. An AMI created in one region (e.g., Mumbai / ap-south-1) is only available in that region. To use it in another region (e.g., North Virginia / us-east-1), you must explicitly copy it there using the Copy AMI action. The copied AMI receives a new, unique AMI ID in the destination region.

questions.question: What is a 'golden AMI' and why do organizations use it?
questions.answer: A golden AMI is a standardized, organization-approved base image containing a pre-hardened OS, all required software, security configurations, and compliance settings. Organizations use it to ensure all servers — across development, testing, and production — start from the same consistent, approved baseline. It is typically updated periodically (e.g., monthly) to incorporate the latest security patches.

questions.question: What are the steps to create a Custom AMI from a running EC2 instance?
questions.answer: (1) Go to EC2 → Instances and select the running instance. (2) Click Actions → Image and Templates → Create Image. (3) Enter an image name and optional description; adjust storage if needed. (4) Click Create Image. AWS creates the AMI in the background (instance keeps running). (5) Navigate to EC2 → AMIs — wait for the status to change from 'pending' to 'available'. (6) Optionally verify the EBS snapshot was created under EC2 → Snapshots.

questions.question: What is the significance of AMI status 'pending' vs 'available'?
questions.answer: 'Pending' means the AMI is still being created and registered by AWS — it cannot be used to launch instances yet. 'Available' means the AMI creation is complete and it is fully ready to use. You should always wait for 'available' before attempting to launch instances from a new AMI.

questions.question: What happens if you deregister an AMI without deleting its EBS snapshot?
questions.answer: The AMI template itself is removed and you can no longer launch instances from it. However, the underlying EBS snapshot that stores the actual disk data continues to exist in your account and continues to incur storage charges (approximately $0.05/GB/month). To fully clean up, you must separately go to EC2 → Snapshots and manually delete the snapshot after deregistering the AMI.

questions.question: Why are custom AMIs useful for auto scaling?
questions.answer: In auto scaling, when traffic spikes, new EC2 instances must be launched quickly. If those instances need Apache, Node.js, application code, and 30+ minutes of manual setup, auto scaling cannot respond fast enough. A custom AMI pre-installs all of that, so a new instance can be launched and fully ready in under 2 minutes — enabling true elastic scaling.

questions.question: Can you launch a t3.micro instance from an AMI that was created on a t3.large instance?
questions.answer: Yes. AMIs and instance types are independent selections. An AMI captures the software configuration — not the compute resources. When launching from an AMI, you choose any compatible instance type (as long as the architecture matches, e.g., both are x86_64). The same AMI can be used to launch t3.micro for testing and m5.xlarge for production.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to evaluate a job offer and decided to decline or negotiate. (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) I received an offer from a startup that seemed promising on the surface — interesting domain, equity offer, flexibility. (Task) I needed to decide whether to accept it or continue looking for a more structured opportunity. (Action) I systematically evaluated the offer: checked for PF structure (not present), requested salary slips format (none automated), asked for exact compensation breakdown (no clear figure provided), and noticed pressure tactics when I asked about opting out of equity. (Result) I declined the offer. Two months later, I joined a structured company with clear HR policies, automated payroll, and a transparent compensation package — which provided better learning and career growth.

questions.question: Your team needs to deploy 20 identical web servers quickly for a product launch. How would you approach this using AWS? (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) A product launch required 20 identically configured web servers within 4 hours. (Task) Set up all 20 servers with Apache, our application code, and configuration — consistently and fast. (Action) I took our fully configured development server, created a custom AMI from it via Actions → Create Image, waited for the AMI to become 'available', then launched 20 EC2 instances simultaneously using that AMI under My AMIs. (Result) All 20 servers were running with identical configuration in under 30 minutes, with zero manual setup per server — saving approximately 10+ hours compared to manual setup.

questions.question: A production server in Mumbai crashed. You need to restore service and also ensure the same configuration is available in North Virginia for failover. What do you do? (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) A production EC2 instance in Mumbai failed, and we needed both immediate recovery and cross-region failover capability. (Task) Restore the server and set up a North Virginia backup. (Action) I located the most recent custom AMI taken from the production server in EC2 → AMIs, launched a new instance from it in Mumbai (restoring service in minutes), then used Actions → Copy AMI to copy it to us-east-1 (North Virginia). Once the copy was available, I launched a standby instance there. (Result) Service was restored in Mumbai in under 10 minutes, and a geographically redundant standby was up in North Virginia within 20 minutes.

questions.question: During a cost audit, you find multiple old AMIs no longer in use, along with their snapshots. How do you clean them up properly? (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) A cost review revealed 15 unused custom AMIs from old projects, each with associated EBS snapshots accumulating storage charges. (Task) Clean up all unused resources completely. (Action) For each AMI: noted the associated snapshot IDs first, then deregistered the AMI via EC2 → AMIs → Actions → Deregister AMI, then navigated to EC2 → Snapshots and deleted each corresponding snapshot. Verified no active instances were still using those AMIs before deregistering. (Result) Removed 15 AMIs and their snapshots, reducing EBS snapshot storage costs by approximately $X per month.

questions.question: A new team member launched an EC2 instance but used a Quick Start AMI instead of the company's golden AMI. What are the risks and how would you address this? (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer launched an instance from a plain Ubuntu Quick Start AMI instead of the company's hardened golden AMI. (Task) Address the compliance and security risk. (Action) Explained that the Quick Start AMI lacks our company's security hardening, required agent installations, and configuration standards. Terminated the non-compliant instance, helped the developer locate the golden AMI under My AMIs, relaunched from the correct AMI, and updated the team's onboarding guide to document the correct AMI ID to always use. (Result) The instance was replaced with a compliant one within 30 minutes; the documentation update prevented similar issues for future team members.

questions.question: Your company is expanding to a new AWS region (Frankfurt) to serve European customers. How do you ensure the same application stack is available there? (STAR)
questions.answer: (Situation) Business decision made to expand to eu-central-1 (Frankfurt) for European customers. (Task) Make our existing application AMI available in Frankfurt. (Action) Went to EC2 → AMIs in the source region, selected our production golden AMI, clicked Actions → Copy AMI, selected eu-central-1 as the destination. After the copy status changed to 'available', launched a new EC2 instance in Frankfurt from the copied AMI and verified the application loaded correctly. (Result) Identical application servers running in Frankfurt within 30 minutes, serving European users with lower latency.

questions.question: How would you implement a monthly AMI rotation policy for a production server?
questions.answer: A monthly AMI rotation policy involves: (1) On a set schedule (e.g., first Sunday of each month), create a new AMI from the production instance after applying OS patches and updates. (2) Name it with a version/date tag (e.g., 'golden-ami-2025-11'). (3) Update Auto Scaling launch templates or launch configurations to point to the new AMI. (4) After confirming the new AMI works correctly with test instances, deregister AMIs older than the retention window (e.g., keep 3 months). (5) Delete associated old snapshots. This ensures all new capacity always starts from a current, patched baseline.

questions.question: Describe AMI pricing — what are you actually charged for?
questions.answer: There is no charge for registering or storing the AMI reference itself. The actual cost comes from the EBS snapshots that back the AMI — charged at approximately $0.05 per GB per month (varies by region). Since EBS snapshots are incremental (only changed blocks are stored after the first snapshot), subsequent snapshots of the same instance are typically smaller and cheaper than the first. You are also charged for any EC2 instances launched from the AMI at the standard EC2 and EBS pricing rates.

questions.question: What is the difference between an AMI and an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: An AMI is a static template or blueprint — it defines what a server will contain but does not run or consume compute resources. An EC2 instance is a live, running server created from an AMI — it consumes CPU, memory, network, and EBS storage, and you are billed for it hourly. You can think of the AMI as the mold and the EC2 instance as the object cast from that mold. One AMI can launch unlimited instances.

questions.question: Why should you copy AMIs to multiple regions for disaster recovery?
questions.answer: If an AWS region experiences an outage, all AMIs in that region are inaccessible. If your only AMI is in the affected region, you cannot rebuild your servers elsewhere. By copying AMIs to at least one other region, you maintain the ability to rebuild your entire environment from scratch in a healthy region during a disaster — minimizing RTO (Recovery Time Objective). This is a core pillar of business continuity planning on AWS.

questions.question: How does AMI architecture (x86_64 vs ARM64) affect instance selection, and what is Graviton's relevance?
questions.answer: AMIs are built for a specific CPU architecture — x86_64 (Intel/AMD) or ARM64 (AWS Graviton). An x86_64 AMI cannot run on an ARM64 instance type (e.g., t4g, m6g, c7g) and vice versa. AWS Graviton instances use ARM64 architecture and offer approximately 20% better price-performance than equivalent x86 instances for many workloads. Organizations maintaining golden AMIs must decide whether to maintain separate x86_64 and ARM64 AMI pipelines or standardize on one architecture. Migrating from x86 to Graviton requires recompiling application binaries and building new ARM64 AMIs.

questions.question: What is EC2 Image Builder and how does it relate to AMIs?
questions.answer: EC2 Image Builder is an AWS service that automates the creation, management, and distribution of custom AMIs. Instead of manually creating AMIs, you define an image pipeline that specifies: the base AMI to start from, software components to install, security hardening tests to run, and the regions to distribute to. Image Builder can be scheduled to run automatically (e.g., monthly) to produce fresh golden AMIs, replacing the manual golden AMI rotation process. It integrates with AWS Organizations for multi-account AMI distribution.

questions.question: How would you design an AMI strategy for a multi-environment (dev/staging/prod) architecture?
questions.answer: A robust multi-environment AMI strategy includes: (1) A base golden AMI maintained by the platform team — contains hardened OS, monitoring agents, security tools. (2) Application-specific AMIs built on top of the golden AMI — contain application code and runtime. (3) Environment-specific configuration injected at launch via EC2 user data or AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store — not baked into the AMI (keeps AMIs portable). (4) Version tagging for all AMIs (e.g., app-ami-v1.2.3). (5) Automated AMI creation via EC2 Image Builder in CI/CD pipelines. (6) AMIs promoted from dev → staging → prod after passing automated tests, rather than rebuilt per environment.

questions.question: What is the difference between using AMIs for scaling vs using EC2 User Data scripts?
questions.answer: AMIs pre-bake all software and configuration — launch time is fast (the instance starts ready), but AMI maintenance is required (update the AMI when software changes). EC2 User Data scripts run at first boot to install and configure software dynamically — launch time is slower (installation happens at boot) but the approach is flexible without needing AMI updates for every change. Best practice: use a hybrid approach — bake stable, slow-changing dependencies into the AMI (OS, runtime, agents) and use User Data for environment-specific configs and rapidly-changing application code. This balances fast launch time with deployment flexibility.

questions.question: How would you ensure compliance and auditability of AMIs across a large organization?
questions.answer: An enterprise AMI compliance strategy should include: (1) Tagging all AMIs with metadata — owner, creation date, version, approved-by, compliance-status. (2) Using AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) to prevent EC2 launches from non-approved AMIs. (3) AWS Config rules to detect running instances not launched from approved AMIs and trigger alerts or auto-remediation. (4) A central AMI registry (maintained via EC2 Image Builder or tagging conventions) that defines which AMI IDs are approved for production. (5) Regular audits using AWS Config or Security Hub to report on AMI compliance status. (6) Automated decommissioning of deprecated AMIs after a defined retention window.
